question: A family walk keeps splitting up because one person walks much faster. What keeps it one walk?
options: Everyone walks at the slowest pace
The group splits into two walks
The faster walker waits at the end
explanation: Looping back means nobody has to be the one being held back and nobody has to be the one slowing everyone down. The fast walker gets extra distance out of the same walk, and the group is never actually apart for long.
author: agent-A

review.notes: Option B ('The group splits into two walks') is the failure state named in the stem offered back as an answer, so it self-eliminates and the item is really a 1-in-3. Replace it with a plausible tactic (e.g. 'The fast walker carries the bag' or 'They walk a loop route with meeting points').

question: Your cousin finishes her first week of moving every day. Which message is she most likely to keep?
options: I knew you could do it
explanation: Three of these could have been sent to anybody, in any week. Naming the actual day says somebody was watching closely enough to notice it. And calling someone a natural quietly suggests the hard days did not count for much.
author: agent-A

review.notes: Guessable without knowledge: the key is the only concrete, specific option and the other three are interchangeable generic praise, so the odd-one-out rule gives it away. The explanation admits this ('Three of these could have been sent to anybody'). Rewrite so at least two distractors are also specific and observational (e.g. 'You looked tired Thursday and went anyway' framed as a worse choice, or a specific but evaluative comment).

question: A household takes a photo after each session. What is that mostly good for later?
explanation: Big days remember themselves. The value of a picture of a completely ordinary Tuesday is that a year later it is the only proof that Tuesday happened at all, and ordinary days are most of what a long habit is made of.
author: agent-A

question: A nine-year-old wants to race an adult in the family. What keeps that worth doing for both of them?
explanation: A head start keeps the finish close, and a close finish is the part that makes a race fun. Letting somebody win says you were not really trying, and children work that out much faster than adults expect them to.
author: agent-A

question: Two people walking and talking usually end up stepping at the same time. Why does that happen?
options: Footsteps echo and set a beat
The taller one sets the rhythm
explanation: Nobody decides to do it. Both walkers make small corrections toward each other until the corrections cancel out, which is the same reason two pendulum clocks on one shelf drift into swinging together.
author: agent-A

review.notes: The stem's premise is stated more firmly than the evidence supports. Spontaneous interpersonal gait synchronisation is real but far from the norm: Zivotofsky and Hausdorff report it in about 50% of treadmill trials and roughly 36% of over-ground walks, and a systematic review notes it 'emerges in only about half of trials' and is dissociable from simple proximity. 'Usually end up stepping at the same time' should become 'often' or 'sometimes', and the item should carry a source given it makes a quantified behavioural claim under `simplified`.

question: A friend two states away wants to keep a daily habit alongside you. What actually makes that work?
options: Doing it at the same hour
Living in the same time zone
explanation: What crosses the distance is the message, not the clock. Two people on opposite schedules doing completely different activities can still hold each other to it, as long as each one knows whether the other went.
author: agent-A

question: A child is copying a movement for the first time. Why is it worth showing it slower than usual?
options: It uses more muscle that way
It makes the set last longer
explanation: Whatever tempo you show is the tempo that gets learned, rushed edges included. Going slowly also gives them time to look at more than one thing, so they can watch the feet on one repeat and the hands on the next.
author: agent-A

question: A house with a toddler in it never gets a quiet half hour. What does moving together look like there?
options: Several short bursts in a day
Waking earlier to fit it in
Taking turns to go out alone
explanation: Movement adds up across a day whether or not it arrived in one block. A household with small children is the clearest case where the all-at-once version was never going to happen, and the scattered version still counts.
author: agent-A

review.notes: Solvable purely by elimination from the stem, with no knowledge required. 'Never gets a quiet half hour' rules out the long session and the earlier wake-up, and 'moving together' rules out taking turns alone, leaving only the key. Either drop the eliminating clause from the stem or make the distractors survive it (e.g. 'A longer session at the weekend only', 'Moving only while the toddler naps').

question: You are partway up a long hill and the person with you is struggling. What helps them most?
options: Walking ahead to set a pace
Pointing out the top is close
explanation: Matching somebody's pace is support they can feel without a word being said. Walking ahead to pace them turns the hill into a gap they now have to close, and the top is usually not as close as the encouraging version claims.
author: agent-A

review.notes: Every one of the four options assumes the struggling person keeps climbing; none offers checking in, slowing to a rest, or turning back. For an audience that includes seniors this quietly teaches push-through as the only option. Add an option that respects the other person's limit, and soften 'helps them most' — this is an editorial judgement, not a ranked finding.

question: What do tag, catch, and dancing have in common that a family workout usually doesn't?
explanation: Catch needs a ball, dancing is usually indoors, and only one of the three keeps score. What all three share is that the activity holds your attention while the effort happens behind your back, so nobody has to be talked into minute nine.
author: agent-A

review.notes: All three distractors are factually false about the named activities and the explanation itself refutes them (catch needs a ball, dancing is not competitive, dancing is usually indoors). A reader who knows nothing about the teaching point eliminates all three from common sense and lands on the key. Rebuild with distractors that are true of tag, catch and dancing but also true of a family workout.

question: Where along a child's long bones does the lengthening actually happen?
options: In the marrow at the center
Near the ends, at growth plates
explanation: Growth plates are cartilage rather than bone, so they show up as gaps on an X-ray of a child's wrist, and a doctor can estimate how much growing is left from what those gaps look like. They harden shut when growing finishes.
author: agent-A

question: A baby has more separate bones than an adult does. What happens to the extra ones?
options: They harden and are then counted
Each one splits as you grow
explanation: A newborn has around 300 separate pieces and an adult about 206. The skull is the clearest case: it arrives as plates with gaps between them, which lets the head through at birth and lets the brain keep growing afterward.
author: agent-A

question: Why do teenagers tend to fall asleep later at night than younger children do?
explanation: The shift starts around puberty and is biological: the sleepy signal simply arrives later in the evening. Teenagers still need roughly as much sleep as they did at eleven. Screens can push bedtime later still, but they are not what started it.
author: agent-A

review.notes: The key and the circadian phase-delay mechanism are sound, but the explanation's claim that 'teenagers still need roughly as much sleep as they did at eleven' conflicts with standard guidance, which sets 9-12 hours for ages 6-12 and 8-10 hours for ages 13-18. Teens do need somewhat less than an eleven-year-old; the point to make is that reduced sleep need is not what pushes bedtime later. Reword that sentence, or cite the guidance if the 'roughly the same' framing is kept.

question: At what point in life does a person usually have the most bone tissue they will ever have?
explanation: After that the body keeps replacing bone but stops adding to the total, so the amount built by then sets the starting point for every decade after it. That is why loading bones with activity matters at both ends of a life, not just the later end.
author: agent-A

question: What tends to happen to the feeling of thirst as somebody gets older?
explanation: The need for water does not shrink; the signal does. That is the reason older adults are often encouraged to drink on some kind of routine rather than waiting until they feel like it, which is the opposite of the usual advice.
author: agent-A

question: Why does a young child heat up faster than an adult during the same game on a hot day?
options: They have no sweat glands yet
They drink less than adults do
More skin area for their size
explanation: A smaller body has more surface compared with the amount inside it, so it picks up heat from hot air more quickly, and children sweat less efficiently than adults on top of that. The shade and the water break matter more for the child than for the adult standing next to them.
author: agent-A

review.notes: The stem's premise is the retired view. The AAP's 2011 policy statement on climatic heat stress revised the earlier position and states that youth do not have a thermoregulatory apparatus inferior to adults' during exercise in the heat when hydration is maintained; the higher surface-area-to-mass ratio is now described as aiding dry heat loss and sweat evaporation, not as a disadvantage. So the key ('More skin area for their size') is the discredited explanation for a comparison that current consensus does not support, and no option in the set is correct. Two distractors are also eliminable without knowledge ('no sweat glands yet', 'hearts beat more slowly'). Keep the shade-and-water message, but build it on something true — e.g. that children are less likely to notice or act on heat and thirst cues than the adult beside them — and mark it `contested` if the comparison is kept at all.

question: A child's resting heart rate is faster than an adult's. What is the main reason?
explanation: A smaller heart moves less blood with each squeeze, so it has to squeeze more often to move the same amount around. A newborn's resting rate can be close to double an adult's, and it settles downward all through childhood.
author: agent-A

question: Why is getting down to the floor and back up worth practicing as people get older?
options: It is a skill that fades unused
It warms the hips up quickly
explanation: Most of the strength and coordination for it is still there. What goes missing is the practice, because adults can spend decades never sitting on a floor at all. People who keep getting down and up keep the pattern available.
author: agent-A

review.notes: Two problems. The explanation's claim that 'most of the strength and coordination for it is still there' and that only practice goes missing is firmer than the evidence and misleading for older readers: difficulty getting off the floor is substantially driven by loss of lower-body strength, power and balance, not disuse alone. Second, the stem's 'worth practicing' telegraphs the key, which is the only option containing 'skill', while the other three are weak. Soften the explanation to 'practice is part of it' and rebuild the distractors.

question: Somebody sleeps the same number of hours as they always did but wakes less refreshed. What changed?
options: Deep sleep takes up less of it
The brain skips the dream stage
explanation: The hours can stay the same while the deepest stretch, the part that does the most repair work, gets shorter. Waking briefly more often through the night pulls in the same direction, even when none of those wakings are remembered.
author: agent-A

question: A toddler learning to walk keeps their feet wide and their arms up. What is that doing for them?
options: It makes them harder to tip
explanation: Wide feet and raised arms are the same trick a tightrope walker uses: a broader base underneath and weight held out to the sides. Both habits fade on their own once balance becomes reliable enough not to need them.
author: agent-A

review.notes: 'It keeps their hands warm' is a throwaway joke distractor, and 'It copies how adults walk' is false on its face to any reader who has watched an adult walk. That leaves the key as the only balance-related option in a question plainly about balance. The science is fine; replace the two dud options with plausible alternatives (e.g. 'It gives them something to grab with', 'It helps them see further ahead').

question: What is the easiest everyday reading of whether you have had enough to drink?
explanation: Pale straw usually means you are fine, and darker usually means go get a drink. Counting cups ignores all the water that arrived in food, and lips dry out from wind and cold whether or not the rest of you is short of water.
author: agent-A

question: Digestion starts in your mouth, before you swallow anything. What is it starting on?
options: It kills germs on the food
It warms the food up first
It adds acid to the food
explanation: Saliva carries an enzyme that goes to work on starch straight away, which is why a plain cracker starts to taste faintly sweet if you hold it in your mouth instead of chewing it. The acid arrives later, in the stomach.
author: agent-A

question: Which part of an apple holds most of its fiber?
explanation: Peeling an apple throws away a large share of its fiber along with the peel. Juice is the same fruit with nearly all the fiber removed, which is why a whole apple keeps you company longer than a glass of apple juice does.
author: agent-A

review.notes: The question asks which part holds 'most' of the fiber, but the flesh is not among the options and actually holds roughly half: a medium apple has about 4.4 g of fiber with the skin and about 2.1 g peeled. 'Most' is firmer than the fact supports. Also guessable with no knowledge, since juice, seeds and core are all eliminable on sight. Reword the stem toward what peeling costs you (which is what the explanation already says correctly) and give the flesh a place in the options.

question: Some vitamins reach you better when the meal has a little oil in it. Why?
options: They dissolve in oil, not water
They are stored in oil only
explanation: Vitamins A, D, E and K travel in oil, so carrots cooked with a little olive oil hand over more of their vitamin A than dry raw ones. Vitamin C is the opposite: it dissolves in water and some of it leaves in the cooking water.
author: agent-A

question: Why are many people thirsty first thing in the morning, having not moved all night?
options: You sweat more asleep than awake
You lose water breathing at night
explanation: Every breath out carries water with it, which you can actually see on a cold morning, and a whole night of breathing adds up. Nothing has gone wrong. You simply have not had a drink in eight hours.
author: agent-A

question: Where does the body keep the fast-release energy it uses at the start of a movement?
explanation: Glycogen is a long chain of glucose that the body can take apart quickly. The liver's share is handed out to the whole body to keep blood sugar steady; the share inside a muscle stays in that muscle and is spent there.
author: agent-A

review.notes: The stem asks for the energy used 'at the start of a movement', and that is the phosphagen system — ATP already in the fiber plus creatine phosphate — which covers roughly the first ten seconds. Glycolysis from glycogen is the next system up, not the one at the start. As written the item teaches a nine-year-old the wrong stage of the energy pathway; this is a simplification that misleads rather than one that omits. Fix by changing the stem to what glycogen actually is (the body's stored carbohydrate fuel, spent once a movement keeps going). Guessability is also weak: calcium-in-bones and iron-in-blood are not energy stores at all and protein is not fast-release, so glycogen is the only option that answers the category of the question.

question: Calcium and vitamin D are usually mentioned together for bones. What is vitamin D doing there?
explanation: Calcium that is eaten but never absorbed passes straight through, so the two work as a pair rather than as two separate items on a list. Skin makes vitamin D from sunlight, and some foods carry it as well.
author: agent-A

question: What is the point of eating something before a long walk first thing in the morning?
options: It keeps you from feeling cold
explanation: The liver spends the night handing out its stored sugar to keep blood supplied, so it starts the morning with less than it went to bed with. Food does not become usable energy the moment it is swallowed either, so earlier is easier.
author: agent-A

question: Your mouth goes dry standing at the start of something you are nervous about. What is happening?
explanation: The body's alert setting pauses jobs that can safely wait, and making saliva is one of them. A dry mouth on a start line is a nervous system doing its job, not a sign that you are short of water.
author: agent-A

review.notes: Most serious item in the sample. The mechanism is right — sympathetic arousal cuts salivary flow — but the closing line, 'A dry mouth on a start line is a nervous system doing its job, not a sign that you are short of water', is a categorical reassurance that a symptom is nothing, with no boundary. Dry mouth genuinely is one of the signs of dehydration, and this app is used by children and by seniors, the group with the most blunted thirst response and the highest dehydration risk. Told this, a hot, under-drunk reader has been given a reason not to drink. The claim must be bounded: nerves can dry your mouth before a start, and if it stays dry once you have settled, or you are hot and sweating, drink anyway. Also, distractor 1 ('You breathe out more water') is partially a real contributing mechanism — nervous mouth-breathing does dry the mouth — so it is not cleanly wrong.

question: Bread, rice, and potatoes are all mostly starch. What does that starch become once it is digested?
explanation: Starch is a long chain of glucose, so all three arrive as the same fuel in the end; what differs between them is everything that comes along with the starch. Fiber is the chain the body cannot take apart, and that one really does pass through.
author: agent-A

question: Where does the extra warmth in a warm-up come from?
options: Blood carrying heat out of your core
Friction between the bones in a joint
Muscles making heat as they work
explanation: Working muscle is a bit wasteful: a lot of the energy it uses leaves as heat rather than movement. That is why you can warm up on a cold morning without the air changing at all.
author: agent-B

question: What does hot weather change about warming up?
options: Nothing, you warm up the same way
It can be shorter, not skipped
It removes the need for one
It should be longer than usual
explanation: Heat loosens skin and surface muscle quickly, but a warm-up is also rehearsal: it is where your body works out the movement before the effort counts. That part does not come free with the weather.
author: agent-B

review.notes: Guessability: the key is the only hedged option among three absolutes ("Nothing...same way", "removes the need", "should be longer"), and its own wording ("not skipped") telegraphs the responsible answer. A reader knowing nothing picks it. Also the explanation's physiology is loose: "heat loosens skin and surface muscle" is not a real mechanism. Rewrite so at least two distractors are genuinely held beliefs stated with the same confidence as the key, and replace the skin/muscle line with the actual point (ambient heat raises tissue temperature but does not rehearse the movement pattern).

question: What separates feeling stiff from feeling sore?
options: Stiffness eases as you move around
Stiffness only happens in the morning
Soreness is always worse than stiffness
They tend to arrive at the same time
explanation: Stiffness is about how a joint feels when it has been still; soreness is about how a muscle feels when you press or load it. Stiffness usually improves within a few minutes of moving. Soreness takes days and does not care that you have got going.
author: agent-B

review.notes: Guessability: two distractors are disqualified by their own absolutes ("only happens in the morning", "always worse than") and the fourth ("arrive at the same time") does not answer the question asked, leaving the key as the only option that states a difference at all. Restate the distractors as plausible differences a reader might actually believe (e.g. "soreness shows up straight away", "stiffness means damage") so the item tests the stiffness/soreness distinction rather than option grammar.

question: You have ten minutes in total. How does a warm-up fit in?
options: Skip it and use all ten on the work
Stretch on the floor for five minutes
Walk briskly for eight of them
Start with an easier version of it
explanation: A warm-up does not have to be a separate activity that eats your ten minutes. The first easy round of the thing you are about to do is a warm-up, and it costs you almost no time at all.
author: agent-B

review.notes: Two of three distractors are throwaways: "skip it" is the bare-dismissal option and "walk briskly for eight of them" leaves two minutes for the work, which no reader will choose. That makes it a coin flip against the one real belief (floor stretching). Replace both with warm-up choices people actually make on a short clock, e.g. "two minutes of arm swings and leg swings" or "a few hard reps to wake the muscles up".

question: What is your body doing in the first couple of minutes of effort?
options: Shifting breathing and blood flow up
Using up the last of yesterday's energy
Waiting for the muscles to unfreeze
Working at its hardest point of the day
explanation: Your muscles ask for more oxygen the instant you start, but breathing and circulation take a minute or two to catch up. That gap is why minute two often feels worse than minute ten, even though you are going the same speed.
author: agent-B

question: You warm up, then sit and talk for twenty minutes. What happened to it?
options: It stays with you for about an hour
It counts as your cool-down instead
It fades, so ease back in again
It works better after a rest
explanation: The warmth and the blood flow drain away faster than people expect. You do not need the whole warm-up again, but the first minute back should look like a beginning, not a continuation.
author: agent-B

review.notes: Only one distractor is a real belief ("stays with you for about an hour"); "counts as your cool-down instead" and "works better after a rest" are not positions anyone holds, so the field collapses to two. The key is also the only option carrying an instruction, which marks it as the sensible answer. Additionally the twenty-minute figure and the implied decay rate are asserted with no source under `simplified` — either soften to "it fades sooner than people expect" or promote to `established` with a warm-up-decay citation.

question: Someone returns to a routine after three weeks off. What does soreness do?
options: It is gone for good after the first time
It comes back, though usually less
It is worse than the very first session
It returns only if the routine changed
explanation: Whatever your body learned the first time around does not vanish in three weeks, but it does fade. Expect an echo of the original soreness rather than a repeat of it, and it is not a sign the time off undid everything.
author: agent-B

review.notes: Guessability: the key is the only qualified option ("though usually less") against "gone for good", "worse than the very first" and "only if the routine changed" — the exact pattern where form, not knowledge, picks the answer. Rewrite so the distractors are hedged too (e.g. "it comes back just as strong" vs "it comes back milder" vs "it comes back only in the muscles you rested"), so the reader has to know the repeated-bout effect fades partially rather than fully.

question: What does a gentle seated routine need before it starts?
options: A full stretch of every muscle
explanation: A warm-up scales to the thing it is warming up for. For a seated routine that means the same movements through a smaller range first, which is also how you find out what your body is offering today.
author: agent-B

review.notes: Goldilocks structure: the key is the moderate option flanked by a dismissal ("Nothing, it is gentle already"), an extreme ("a full stretch of every muscle") and a mismatch ("five minutes of brisk walking", which is also the wrong recommendation to put in front of someone doing a seated routine precisely because walking is hard for them). Replace the distractors with warm-up choices that are all defensible in scale, so the item tests the scaling principle rather than spotting the middle answer.

question: You are sore in a muscle you did not know you had. What does that mean?
options: You used it in an unfamiliar way
That muscle was weak to begin with
explanation: Most muscles go unnoticed because nothing has ever asked them to work in that direction. A new movement finds them, and the soreness is really just an introduction.
author: agent-B

review.notes: The item explicitly marks "You injured something small there" as wrong and the explanation closes the door on injury ("the soreness is really just an introduction") without giving the reader any way to tell delayed muscle soreness from a strain. For a mixed child/senior audience that is a rule-out with no test attached. Add the distinguishing detail to the explanation — soreness that arrives hours later, is spread across a muscle and eases with gentle movement, versus pain that came on suddenly during the movement, is sharp, or is on one side only — and reword the distractor so ruling it out teaches that difference.

question: Two people do the same new workout. One is sore after, one is not. What does that show?
options: The sore one worked much harder
One of them warmed up better
Mostly how new it was to each
explanation: Soreness tracks unfamiliarity far more than it tracks effort, and people differ a lot in how much they get from the same work. It is a poor way to compare two people and a poor way to grade yourself.
author: agent-B

review.notes: Two problems. (1) Internal contradiction: the stem stipulates 'the same NEW workout', i.e. novelty held constant, and the key then says the difference is 'mostly how new it was to each'. Under the stem's own premise that is the one factor ruled out. The explanation's second clause — that people differ a lot in response to the same work — is the honest answer and is not what the key says. DOMS high/low responder variation to identical unaccustomed eccentric work is large and well documented, so 'mostly novelty' is stated more firmly than the evidence supports. (2) Textbook guessability: the key is the only hedged option ('Mostly...') against three absolutes ('much harder', 'better', 'must be different'), and option 4 flags itself as wrong with 'must'. The anti-comparison message is good and worth keeping; the stem and option set need rebuilding.

question: What matters most when picking shoes to walk in?
options: That they match your arch type
That they fit and you can move
That they have the most cushion
That they are under a year old
explanation: Arch-matching charts and replacement schedules sell a lot of shoes, and the evidence behind them is thin. Shoes that fit, stay on, and let your foot bend cover most of what actually matters.
author: agent-B

question: You are learning a new movement and want to know if you have it right. What helps most?
options: Go by how the movement feels
Count how many you can do
Watch the video one more time
Record it and watch it back
explanation: When a movement is new, the feel of it is the least reliable thing about it: your sense of where your limbs are has not caught up yet. Seeing yourself from outside closes that gap in one go.
author: agent-B

question: Which trip hazard at home is the easiest one to miss?
options: A rug with a curled edge
A high step at the door
explanation: The dramatic hazards get handled, because they look like hazards. A flat rug edge sits at ankle height, matches the floor, and has been there so long that nobody sees it any more.
author: agent-B

review.notes: The key is not uniquely correct. A wet bathroom floor is transparent and routinely invisible until you are standing on it, so it is at least as 'easy to miss' as a curled rug edge — a distractor that competes with the key on the exact axis the stem asks about. Separately the item is close to tautological: the stem asks which hazard is subtle and the rug edge is the only option that is not a famously conspicuous hazard, so a reader who knows nothing can eliminate the other three on the wording alone. Stated as 'simplified' with no source, but 'the easiest one to miss' is a superlative comparative judgment, not a simplification of a known fact. Either narrow the stem to something checkable (e.g. what fall data actually implicates in the home) or rewrite so the distractors are also low-salience hazards.

question: A watch shows a heart rate above the 'maximum' for your age. What is the sensible read?
options: You went past a safe ceiling
A high number means you are fit
Your heart is working too hard
explanation: The age formula is an average with a wide spread around it, so plenty of ordinary people sit above their own number. Wrist readings also jump. How you actually feel is the better instrument.
author: agent-B

review.notes: Safety framing. The item tells a reader — including seniors — that a heart rate above the age-predicted maximum is not worth attending to, and offers "how you actually feel is the better instrument" as the whole answer. That is reassurance functioning as medical advice, with no boundary. Keep the (correct) point that 220-minus-age is a population average with a wide spread, but add the line that stops it being advice: chest pain, dizziness, feeling faint or a rate that will not settle are reasons to stop and get checked, whatever the number says. Distractors also need work — two of the three are alarm framings, leaving the key as the only skeptical option.

question: Why is it easy to end up short of water on a cold day?
options: Cold water is harder to absorb
Cold makes you feel less thirsty
The body stores less in the cold
You sweat the same as in summer
explanation: Cold blunts thirst, and you are also losing water with every breath you can see in front of you. Nothing about the day feels like a hot one, so nobody thinks to drink.
author: agent-B

question: Your form gets sloppy on the last few reps. What is that a sign of?
options: A warm-up that was far too short
A movement too advanced for now
The point where the gains happen
The muscle is out of steam
explanation: Quality falling off is the clearest signal a muscle gives that it is done. Stopping there costs you almost nothing, because the messy reps were never the ones doing the work.
author: agent-B

review.notes: Firmness beyond the evidence in the explanation: "stopping there costs you almost nothing, because the messy reps were never the ones doing the work" states as settled something the training literature actively disputes — proximity to failure is one of the better-supported drivers of adaptation, and the final hard reps are generally held to contribute most. The stop-when-form-degrades message is good and worth keeping; rest it on the real reason (a rep you cannot control is the one that hurts you, and the stimulus you lose is small) rather than on a claim that those reps do nothing.

question: Why do people who feel steady still use the handrail on stairs?
options: It takes some weight off the knees
It is there for the unplanned slip
It keeps you walking more slowly
It stops your arms from swinging
explanation: A handrail is not support for people who need support. It is a thing to catch that you do not have to think about, and you only find out you needed it after you already needed it.
author: agent-B

review.notes: This is the safety-item failure mode named in the review brief: "It is there for the unplanned slip" is the only plausible option. "Keeps you walking more slowly" and "stops your arms from swinging" are not beliefs anyone holds, and the remaining distractor (weight off the knees) is the only competition. Replace them with genuinely tempting wrong beliefs — that handrails are for people who are unsteady, that using one makes your balance worse over time, that it only matters going down — so the item tests why a steady person still uses it.

question: You need a chair to hold for a standing exercise. Which chair is the wrong one?
explanation: A rolling chair moves at exactly the moment you want something not to. Cushions, arms and back height change nothing about whether it holds still, which is the only job you are giving it.
author: agent-B

review.notes: Tests nothing. A chair on wheels is obviously the unsafe one and the other three options (arms, no cushion, tall back) are self-evidently harmless, so any reader gets this at 100% with zero knowledge. The explanation even concedes the point ("cushions, arms and back height change nothing"). Rebuild with four chairs that could all arguably be wrong — one that is too low to reach without stooping, a light folding chair, one positioned so you have to lean to reach it, one on carpet versus a slick floor — and make the answer turn on whether it stays put under load.

question: A child wants to lift something heavy. What matters more than the weight?
options: How many times they lift it
explanation: Can they pick it up, carry it and set it down without it getting away from them? A load under control is a load their body can learn from. One that is steering them is the one that causes trouble.
author: agent-B

review.notes: Safety. The item is addressed to children, encourages lifting something heavy, and explicitly marks "whether their back stays straight" as the wrong answer — which reads to a nine-year-old as technique not mattering. It also has no adult-present framing anywhere. Keep control as the answer if you like, but the explanation must not leave technique discredited (control includes keeping the load close and the spine in a position you chose, not one the weight chose), and the scenario needs a grown-up in it.

question: What happens as a walking route becomes very familiar?
options: Your stride gets shorter over time
You notice more of the details
Your pace stops changing at all
explanation: Walking a known route hands the job to autopilot, which is efficient and slightly careless. The curb that has been there for years is exactly the one nobody looks at any more.
author: agent-B

review.notes: Stem-key word match: the question says "becomes very familiar" and the key says "on familiar ground" — the only option that echoes the stem, which is enough to pick it without knowing anything. The other three are specific mechanical claims about stride and pace that no reader will prefer. Reword the key so it does not repeat the stem's vocabulary, and make the distractors about attention too (e.g. "you scan further ahead", "you spot changes faster") so the item tests automaticity rather than word matching.

question: What does slowing a movement down do to it?
options: Makes it easier on the muscle
explanation: The muscle is under load for the whole time you are moving, so taking four seconds instead of one roughly quadruples that. It is the simplest way to make a movement harder when you have nothing to add to it.
author: agent-B

review.notes: Two firmness problems in one explanation, both under `simplified` with no source: "roughly quadruples" is a quantified claim (and it is wrong as stated — a four-second rep does not quadruple the stimulus, only the duration, and slower tempo usually means less total load moved), and "the simplest way to make a movement harder" is a superlative. Time under tension as a driver of adaptation is also weaker than the text implies. Recast as the experiential truth — slowing down removes momentum, so the muscle does more of the work — and drop both the multiplier and the superlative.

question: What does using a movement's full range add?
options: A faster set, with less effort
Less work for the muscle overall
More reps before you get tired
explanation: Muscles get stronger mostly in the positions you train them in. Cutting a movement short builds strength in the middle of the range and leaves the ends, which are the positions real life keeps putting you in.
author: agent-B

review.notes: All three distractors claim full range makes the work easier or faster ("less effort", "less work overall", "more reps before you get tired"), so the key is the only option offering a benefit and the only one a reader would ever pick. Replace them with plausible alternative benefits that are wrong here — more flexibility only, faster results, less soreness — so the item actually tests the position-specificity point the explanation makes.

question: Can strength work make you more flexible?
options: Yes, if you also hold stretches
explanation: A muscle loaded through its whole range is being asked to produce force in a long position, which is most of what a stretch asks for too. The old idea that lifting makes you stiff came from watching people train through half a range.
author: agent-B

review.notes: The core claim is defensible, but the closing sentence — "the old idea that lifting makes you stiff came from watching people train through half a range" — is an invented origin story presented as fact, with no source. Cut it or mark it as a guess. Separately, "Yes, full-range work does it" is a firm answer to a question the evidence answers as "resistance training through full range improves range of motion about as much as stretching does in the studies we have"; either carry that hedge in the explanation or promote the item to `established` with the systematic-review citation. Two distractors are also disqualified by their own absolutes ("always", "only").

question: Why is one arm usually a little stronger than the other?
options: It gets more use day to day
explanation: You open doors, carry bags and throw with one side without deciding to, and that adds up to years of extra practice. Which is also why the gap narrows once the quieter side gets its own turn.
author: agent-B

question: What is the rest between sets for?
options: Letting the muscle refuel a bit
Giving the muscle time to grow
explanation: Muscles run the first part of a hard set on a fast-burning fuel they keep on site, and it takes a minute or two to restock. Rest too little and the next set is limited by fuel rather than by strength.
author: agent-B

question: How many days a week of muscle-strengthening activity do U.S. guidelines suggest for adults?
explanation: The guideline says at least two days, and it is a floor rather than a target. It also does not say what kind: carrying, climbing and bodyweight movements all count as strengthening.
author: agent-B

review.notes: Citation resolves and supports the answer: the CDC page states adults need "at least 2 days of muscle-strengthening activity each week". But the explanation then says the guideline "does not say what kind", and the same page does specify it — activities that "work all major muscle groups (legs, hips, back, abdomen, chest, shoulders, and arms)". Under `established` the explanation has to stay inside the source. The follow-on claim that "carrying, climbing and bodyweight movements all count" is the item's own assertion, not the CDC's, and carrying groceries in particular does not cover all major muscle groups. Rewrite the second sentence to state what the guideline actually specifies, or drop it.

question: One arm is in a cast. What does training the other arm do for it?
options: It tires the resting arm out
explanation: Strength is partly a skill held in the nervous system, and that part is not fully one-sided. The resting limb keeps more than it would have if nothing was being trained at all.
author: agent-B

question: Two people do the same stretches for months, and only one can touch their toes. Why?
options: Only one bothered to warm up
explanation: How far your fingers get depends on the length of your arms, legs and back and the shape of your hip sockets, none of which a routine changes. Compare your own reach over time; comparing it to somebody else's tells you almost nothing.
author: agent-B

question: Why does holding a plank get harder when nothing is moving?
options: Muscle fibers tire and hand over
Your bones take more of the load
explanation: In a hold, your fibers take turns rather than all pulling at once. As the rested ones run out, the same position needs more of what is left, which is why second forty-five feels nothing like second five.
author: agent-B

review.notes: Distractors are too weak — "your bones take more of the load" and "the muscle slowly stretches out" are not beliefs a reader holds, so the key is the only fatigue explanation on offer for a question that plainly asks about fatigue. The mechanism is also stated more firmly than it is settled: motor-unit rotation ("fibers take turns") is a teaching model that holds at low forces and is disputed at the forces a plank involves, where added recruitment and rising firing rate matter more. Soften the mechanism and give the distractors competing fatigue accounts (e.g. "the core gives out before the shoulders", "you start holding the position less well") so the item discriminates.

question: Why do strength gains slow down after the first couple of months?
options: The muscle has reached its limit
The exercises get stale to you
You stop trying as hard by then
explanation: Early on your body is learning the movement, which is quick. After that it has to actually build, which is slow. The slowdown is a change of gear, not a sign anything went wrong.
author: agent-B

question: What does brain imaging show about brain activity?
options: Every region does something across a day
Roughly a tenth of it ever switches on
One hemisphere runs while the other rests
Activity stops in areas you rarely use
explanation: Different jobs light up different areas minute to minute, and over a day the whole thing gets used — though never every cell at once, which would be a seizure. The ten percent line was never a research finding.
author: agent-C

question: Which body parts get the biggest share of your brain's movement map?
explanation: Brain space is handed out by how finely a part has to be controlled, not by how big it is. Your thigh is enormous and gets a sliver; your lips and fingertips get a wide stretch of cortex.
author: agent-C

question: Which side of your brain does most of the steering when you move your right hand?
explanation: Most movement nerves cross over on their way down, so each half of the brain mainly runs the opposite half of the body. Nobody is certain why the wiring crosses, but it does in nearly every animal with a backbone.
author: agent-C

question: Why is it so hard to tickle yourself?
options: Your fingers go numb when you try
Tickle nerves switch off in your hands
You cannot reach the ticklish spots
Your brain predicts your own touch
explanation: Your brain sends a copy of every movement order over to the touch areas, so the sensation arrives already expected and gets turned down. Surprise is most of what tickling is.
author: agent-C

question: Why is patting your head while rubbing your stomach tricky?
options: Your arms share one nerve to the brain
The two rhythms pull toward each other
The brain can plan only one arm at a time
Circles take longer than pats to learn
explanation: Two different patterns running at once tend to blend, and both hands drift toward doing the same thing. People who get it usually slow right down and let each hand start on its own.
author: agent-C

question: When you lift one arm quickly, which muscles fire first?
explanation: Your body braces before it moves, because swinging an arm up would otherwise tip you forward. The bracing happens a fraction of a second early and you never notice ordering it.
author: agent-C

question: What happens to most people's walking while they do hard mental math?
options: It slows and gets less even
It speeds up without them noticing
explanation: Walking looks automatic but still borrows attention, and a demanding thought takes some of it back. Researchers use that slow-down as a way to measure how automatic someone's walking has become.
author: agent-C

question: What happens when you return to a skill you learned years ago and dropped?
options: It has to be learned again from zero
It comes back quicker than before
It returns only with a coach's help
It feels new for about the same time
explanation: The pattern was never erased, only left alone, so practice is rebuilding instead of building. Riding a bike is the famous case, but it holds for swimming strokes and instruments too.
author: agent-C

question: Do people react faster to a sound or to a flash of light?
options: To the light, by a lot
explanation: Sound reaches the parts of the brain that trigger a movement through a shorter chain than vision does. The gap is only a few hundredths of a second, which is part of why sprint races start with a gun and not a lamp.
author: agent-C

review.notes: The answer is right but the explanation gives the wrong mechanism. It says sound wins because it reaches motor areas 'through a shorter chain than vision does'. The dominant cause is that hearing transduces mechanically in about a millisecond while the retina runs a multi-step biochemical cascade that costs tens of milliseconds; pathway length is secondary. Rewrite along the lines of 'the ear turns sound into a nerve signal almost instantly, while the eye has to run a slower chemical chain first'. Also consider reworking the options: 'light' appears twice and 'sound' once, so the odd-one-out is a structural tell.

question: What do your movement areas do while you watch someone else move?
options: They shut down while you watch
They wait until it is your turn
They quietly light up as well
They run the motion in your muscles
explanation: Watching a movement partly rehearses it, which is part of why showing teaches faster than telling. It is not the same as doing it — the final order to actually contract gets held back.
author: agent-C

question: Which part of your tongue picks up sweet tastes?
options: Every part that has taste buds
Only the tip at the front
The middle, where it is smooth
explanation: The taste map in old textbooks came from a chart of small differences in sensitivity that got redrawn as separate zones. Every taste-bud region answers to all the basic tastes, including the roof of your mouth.
author: agent-C

question: Which of these is a real sense your body has, beyond the famous five?
options: A sense of your own balance
A sense of the time of year
explanation: The five-senses list comes from ancient philosophy rather than biology. Balance has its own organ in the inner ear, and temperature and limb position are separate systems again — researchers disagree about where the list should end.
author: agent-C

review.notes: Guessable to the point of being free. Two distractors ('a sense of magnetic north', 'a sense of nearby metal') are things no reader believes a human has, so the key is the only survivable option and a nine-year-old who knows nothing scores it. Replace them with senses people genuinely argue about or would not expect, e.g. a sense of how full your stomach is, a sense of how hard a muscle is pulling, a sense of your own heartbeat — all real, which forces the reader to think about what 'a sense' means instead of eliminating jokes. Separately, note that human magnetoreception is an active research question, so flatly listing it as not-a-sense is shakier than the item implies.

question: Why does your recorded voice sound wrong to you?
options: Microphones cut the lowest notes out
You hear your voice a beat delayed
You normally hear it through bone too
Recordings raise every pitch a little
explanation: Speaking sends sound to your ears two ways, through the air and through the bones of your skull, and the bone path adds a depth the recording never had. Everybody else has only ever heard the air version.
author: agent-C

question: Why does food taste flat when your nose is blocked?
options: A blocked nose dries the tongue
Much of flavor is really smell
The tongue cools and slows down
explanation: Your tongue reports only a handful of basics — sweet, salty, sour, bitter, savory. Everything that makes strawberry taste like strawberry travels up the back of your nose while you chew.
author: agent-C

question: What is true about catching a yawn from somebody?
options: People stop catching them by ten
explanation: Catching yawns tends to appear around age four or five rather than at birth, and dogs will yawn back at a person they know well. Why yawns exist at all is still being argued over.
author: agent-C

review.notes: The key states a contested finding as settled fact. Contagious yawning in dogs has a mixed replication record: the original 2008 report was followed by failures to replicate and by disputes over whether familiarity with the person matters at all. The item's own explanation hedges the wrong thing — it hedges why yawns exist, which nobody needed hedged, while asserting 'dogs will yawn back at a person they know well' flat out. Either mark the item contested and say so in the text ('some studies find dogs catch yawns from people, others have not been able to repeat it'), or move the key to the age finding, which is much better supported: contagious yawning appears around four or five rather than being present at birth.

question: What happens to what you see during a blink?
options: You see a brief flash of gray
Your eyes keep a faint image
explanation: Vision gets dialed down just before the lid moves and picked back up after, so the darkness never reaches awareness. The same trick hides the blur every time your eyes jump from word to word.
author: agent-C

review.notes: The key and explanation are sound, but distractor 4, 'Light still passes the eyelid', is literally true — eyelids transmit a small amount of light, which is why closed eyes look red in sunshine. A reader who knows that has two defensible answers and no way to choose. Replace it with something false, e.g. 'Your eyes scan ahead while shut'. Minor second point: the explanation says vision is dialled down 'just before the lid moves and picked back up after' — fine as written, but do not let an edit tighten this into a claim that you see nothing at all during a blink.

question: What is a person's normal body temperature?
options: A peak right after waking up
A figure that swings all day
explanation: Readings run lower in the early morning and higher in the late afternoon, and healthy people differ from one another. The famous single figure was an average taken in the 1800s.
author: agent-C

question: Where does digestion actually begin?
explanation: Saliva carries an enzyme that starts breaking starch apart before you swallow. Hold a plain cracker on your tongue without chewing and you can taste it turn sweet.
author: agent-C

review.notes: Cross-author duplicate: teaches the same fact as SF-TRV-000426 (digestion begins in the mouth), written independently by a different author who could not see the other batch. 426 is kept because it teaches the mechanism (starch/amylase) rather than only the location. The process fix is to give parallel authors each other's stems, not just the librarys.

question: What job do your eyebrows do besides showing how you feel?
explanation: The hairs run sideways, out toward your temples, so anything running down your forehead gets sent around your eyes instead of into them. Eyelashes are the ones that handle dust.
author: agent-C

review.notes: Overstated firmness plus a false dichotomy. Sweat/rain diversion is a plausible and widely repeated hypothesis about eyebrows, not an established function; the better-evidenced line of work treats eyebrows primarily as social/expressive signalling and the diversion role as secondary and inferred. The item states it flatly as 'the' job. Worse, the explanation's 'Eyelashes are the ones that handle dust' marks distractor 3 wrong when eyebrows do in fact intercept falling debris as well — so the item declares one option uniquely correct against a distractor that is partly true. Needs hedging ('probably helps steer...') and removal of the eyelash exclusivity claim, or a real source.

question: Why do your eyes water when somebody cuts an onion?
options: A gas from the onion stings
explanation: Cutting breaks open cells that had been keeping two chemicals apart, and what they make drifts up as a gas that irritates the surface of the eye. Chilling the onion first slows the reaction down.
author: agent-C

question: How does a newborn's number of bones compare with an adult's?
explanation: Many bones start out as separate pieces with cartilage between them and knit together through childhood — the skull and the hip bones both do it. The soft spots on a baby's head are that process still unfinished.
author: agent-C

question: Which bone in your body connects to no other bone?
explanation: The hyoid is a small U-shaped bone in the neck, held in place by muscles and ligaments alone. It anchors your tongue and the muscles you swallow with.
author: agent-C

question: What shape does a healthy spine make from the side?
explanation: The curves work like a spring, spreading the load of your head and letting the column flex. A perfectly straight stack would pass the shock of every step straight up to your skull.
author: agent-C

question: What moves food along inside you after you swallow?
options: The same muscle as your arms
explanation: The tube has its own muscle layers that squeeze in waves, working whether or not you think about them. It is why astronauts can swallow perfectly well with no gravity to help.
author: agent-C

question: Why does your elbow need a muscle on each side?
options: One side works, one side rests
Each side handles half the weight
Muscles can pull but not push
Bone would snap under one muscle
explanation: A muscle shortens; that is its only move. Bending takes one muscle pulling, and straightening takes a different one on the opposite side pulling the other way.
author: agent-C

question: What is different about the muscle fibers used for sprinting?
options: They are longer than the others
They sit closer to the skin
They contract fast and tire fast
explanation: Everyone carries a mix of quick-tiring and slow-tiring fibers inside the same muscle, and which ones get called on depends on how hard and how fast the job is. The proportions differ from person to person.
author: agent-C

review.notes: The content is accurate and well hedged, but the question hands the reader the answer: 'sprinting' is obviously fast and the key is the only option containing the word 'fast'. A nine-year-old who knows nothing about fibre types matches the words and scores. Fix by removing the lexical link — ask instead what is different about the fibres you use for a short all-out effort compared with the ones you use on a long walk, or reword the key so the giveaway word is gone (e.g. 'They run out of fuel quickly').

question: Which of these can rebuild itself after it is damaged?
explanation: Bone is living tissue with its own blood supply, so cells knit a break back together. Enamel was built by cells that die off once the tooth is finished, leaving nothing behind to do repairs.
author: agent-C

review.notes: Structural giveaway: three of the four options are teeth and the key is the only bone, so the odd one out is the answer without any knowledge — and 'broken bones heal' is already common knowledge for this age group. The teaching is entirely in the explanation, not in the question. Rework so the choice is genuinely between candidates, e.g. all four options tissues that differ in repair ability (a cracked bone, tooth enamel, the lens of the eye, a fingernail), or invert the question to ask which of four damaged things cannot rebuild itself.

question: Where does the warmth come from when you start moving?
explanation: Muscles are not tidy machines — a good share of the energy they use leaves as heat instead of movement. Shivering is your body putting that same inefficiency to work on purpose.
author: agent-C

question: What is unusual about your lowest pair of ribs?
explanation: Most ribs curve around and join the breastbone through cartilage, but the bottom pair simply ends in the muscle of your side. They are called floating ribs, and they are part of why your lower trunk twists more easily than your chest.
author: agent-C

review.notes: Two factual problems in the explanation. (1) There are normally two pairs of floating ribs, 11 and 12, not one. The item repeatedly says 'the bottom pair' and then names that single pair 'floating ribs', which teaches the wrong anatomy. It also blurs the false ribs: ribs 8 to 10 do not reach the breastbone directly either, they join the cartilage above, so 'most ribs curve around and join the breastbone through cartilage' is loose at best. (2) 'they are part of why your lower trunk twists more easily than your chest' looks backwards — the lumbar spine is the most rotation-restricted region of the spine (roughly 5 to 13 degrees total) while the thoracic spine rotates far more (roughly 35 degrees), the rib cage notwithstanding. Either drop that sentence or replace it with something defensible about the lower ribs being free to move with breathing. Fix the rib count first; the key itself ('they reach no breastbone') is true and can stay.

question: Why can your eyes aim more precisely than your legs can?
explanation: A nerve cell and the muscle fibers it controls fire together as one unit, so the fewer fibers per nerve, the finer the adjustment possible. Eye muscles run a handful each; a big leg muscle can run many hundreds at once.
author: agent-C
